stimuli.title: Three Digits for Help: How 911 Came to Be
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] For most of the twentieth century, a person facing an emergency in the United States had to know the right number to call. A fire might require one seven-digit number, the police another, and an ambulance service a third. In many towns the simplest choice was to dial “0” and ask the telephone operator for help, but operators handled every kind of request, and a caller reporting a house fire might wait behind someone asking for a long-distance connection. In a large metropolitan area, residents could face dozens of different emergency numbers, depending on which side of a city or county line they lived on.

[2] Other countries had already found a simpler approach. In 1937, London introduced 999, a single number that rang through to operators who could send police, firefighters, or an ambulance. Calls for a similar system in the United States began in 1957, when a national association of fire chiefs recommended one number for reporting fires. The idea gained real momentum a decade later. In 1967, a presidential commission studying crime and law enforcement urged the country to adopt a single number for reporting all emergencies.

[3] The telephone industry then had to choose the digits. In January 1968, AT&T, which operated most of the nation's phone lines, announced that the number would be 9-1-1. The combination had practical advantages. It was short and easy to remember. It had also never been used as an area code or as the first three digits of a local phone number, so it would not conflict with numbers already in service. On the rotary-dial phones of the time, it could be dialed fairly quickly while still being unlikely to be dialed by accident.

[4] The first 911 call, however, did not travel over an AT&T line. A small independent company, the Alabama Telephone Company, raced to beat the giant to the milestone. Its crews worked quickly to rewire equipment in the town of Haleyville, Alabama, and on February 16, 1968, a state official placed a call from city hall to a congressman waiting at the local police station. The call was ceremonial, but it proved the system could work.

[5] Spreading the service across the country took far longer than that first call. Each city or county had to decide who would answer 911 calls, build a call center, and pay for equipment and trained staff. Many communities funded their systems with a small monthly fee added to telephone bills. Progress was uneven: some large cities adopted 911 within a few years, while many rural areas waited until the 1990s or later.

[6] As the service spread, engineers worked to make it smarter. Early 911 told a dispatcher nothing about the caller; if a frightened person could not speak or did not know the address, help could be delayed. Enhanced 911, developed during the 1970s and 1980s, automatically displayed the caller's phone number and the street address linked to that line. A dispatcher could now send help to a caller who had collapsed before saying a word.

[7] Cell phones created a new problem. A mobile phone has no fixed address, so the location information that made Enhanced 911 so useful disappeared when callers left their landlines behind. In 1999, Congress passed a law designating 911 as the universal emergency number for all telephone service, and around the same time federal regulators began requiring wireless carriers, in stages, to send location data with emergency calls. That work continues today, because a cell phone's reported location can still be off by many yards, particularly inside tall buildings.

[8] Today, call centers across the country handle an estimated 240 million 911 calls each year, and most of those calls come from cell phones. In many areas, people who cannot safely speak can now send a text message to 911. In 2022, the nation also launched 988, a separate three-digit number for people experiencing a mental health crisis, so that those callers can reach trained counselors. More than half a century after Haleyville, the basic promise of 911 remains the same: in the worst moment of a person's life, no one should have to search for the right number.

stimuli.title: Smoke on the Far Ridge
stimuli.source: Original story written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] From the catwalk of the Juniper Butte lookout, the whole forest looked like a rumpled green blanket somebody had tossed over the mountains and forgotten to straighten. Nell Okerlund had been staring at it for six weeks now, through morning haze and afternoon thunderheads, and she was beginning to believe she knew every fold.

[2] Before this summer, the tower had belonged to Walt Brannigan for thirty-one seasons. He had trained her in June, walking her around the fire finder, the round metal table in the center of the cab with its map and sighting ring, and telling her the names of the ridges as if he were introducing old neighbors. “That's Coyote Shoulder. That's the Dutchman. That bald spot is Sweeney's Burn, from '88.” Then his eyes had grown too cloudy for the work, and the district had sent him down the mountain with a cake and a plaque, and now it was just Nell, the radio, and a logbook full of his square handwriting.

[3] At 4:10 on a hot afternoon in late July, she saw it: a thin gray thread rising beyond the Dutchman. It wavered, leaned, thinned to nothing, and appeared again.

[4] Nell's stomach tightened. Dust, she told herself. A logging truck on the forest road. Walt had warned her about that. “Half the smokes a new lookout calls in are dust,” he'd said. “Dispatch will be polite about it. Then they'll tell the whole district.” She had already called in one false smoke in her second week, steam rising from a hot spring after rain, and she could still hear the patient voice on the radio: Copy that, Juniper, we'll make a note.

[5] She lifted the binoculars. The thread was bluer than dust, and it did not drift the way dust drifted, sideways and low. It climbed. But it was so small. If she called it in and it turned out to be nothing, she would be the girl who cried smoke, twice.

[6] She opened Walt's logbook instead, flipping back through years of entries, looking for a sign of what he would do. July 1994: Smoke, Dutchman, NE slope. Reported 15:20. Lightning strike. Crew on scene 17:45. August 2003: Possible smoke, Dutchman. Watched 20 min. Thought dust. Not reported. Below that, in different ink, as if added later: Not dust. Should have called it. Better a dozen false alarms than one late one.

[7] Nell read the line twice. She had always imagined Walt as someone who was never wrong, someone who simply knew. It had not occurred to her that he had stood in this same spot, squinting at the same ridge, unsure.

[8] She put the logbook down and bent over the fire finder. She swung the sighting ring until the crosshair lined up with the thread of smoke, read the bearing, checked it, and read it again. Then she picked up the radio.

[9] “Dispatch, Juniper Butte. I have a smoke, bearing two-one-four, approximately six miles, just beyond the Dutchman. Small, bluish gray, steady. Will advise.”

[10] There was a pause, and then the same patient voice: “Copy, Juniper. Sending an engine to check it out.”

[11] For the next forty minutes Nell watched the thread thicken into a column and then, as the engine crew reached it, flatten and fade. At 5:05 the radio crackled again. A lightning strike from the storm two nights earlier had been smoldering in a dead snag. Quarter acre, contained. Good catch, Juniper.

[12] That evening she opened the logbook to a fresh page. She wrote the date, the time, the bearing, and the outcome in her own handwriting, which was rounder and less certain-looking than Walt's. Then, after a moment, she turned back to August 2003 and read his note one more time before she closed the book and went out onto the catwalk to watch the light leave the ridges, one fold at a time.

stimuli.title: Tuition-Free Community College Is an Investment That Pays Off
stimuli.source: Original argument written for KCE GED Prep. Delford County is fictional.
stimuli.html:
For most of the last century, a high school diploma was enough to land a steady job with decent pay. That is no longer true. Employers in health care, advanced manufacturing, information technology, and the skilled trades increasingly expect workers to have training beyond high school. Community colleges provide exactly that training, close to home and at a fraction of the cost of a university. Making community college tuition-free would open that door to every graduate, and the evidence shows it is a smart use of public money.

Start with what a two-year credential is worth. According to federal labor statistics, workers whose highest degree is an associate degree earn about $160 more per week, on average, than workers with only a high school diploma, and they have a lower unemployment rate. Over a 40-year career, $160 a week adds up to more than $300,000. Those higher earnings also mean more tax revenue and less need for public assistance.

Cost keeps many qualified students from collecting that reward. Tuition at a community college averages roughly $4,000 a year. That is modest compared with a university, but it is a real barrier for a family living paycheck to paycheck. Federal grants help the lowest-income students, yet many working families earn too much to qualify and too little to pay comfortably.

Places that have removed the barrier have seen results. When Delford County began covering tuition for recent high school graduates at its community college in 2019, enrollment from that group rose 31 percent within two years. More important, the share of students who earned a degree or certificate within three years climbed from 24 percent to 33 percent, according to the college's annual reports. Counselors there say the simple message “college is free” reached students who had never imagined themselves in a classroom after high school.

The program is not expensive. It costs Delford County about $3.1 million a year, less than 1 percent of its budget. An analysis by the county's finance office estimated that the higher earnings of the program's additional graduates will return more than that amount in local taxes within ten years.

Critics warn that some students will enroll and then drop out. Some will. But the Delford data show that completion rose, not fell, once tuition was removed. A nation that wants a skilled workforce should stop charging admission to the place where so many workers get their skills. Tuition-free community college is not a handout; it is an investment that pays for itself.

stimuli.title: Free Tuition Comes With a Hidden Price Tag
stimuli.source: Original argument written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Supporters of tuition-free community college like to say that it “pays for itself.” Nothing pays for itself. Every dollar spent on free tuition is a dollar taken from taxpayers, including the many working people who never went to college and never will. Before we hand them that bill, we should ask whether free tuition actually solves the problems students face.

It does not. For many low-income students, federal grants already cover the full cost of community college tuition. That means a free-tuition program sends much of its money to families who could afford to pay their own way. It is a benefit aimed at the wrong people.

Tuition is also only a small part of what college costs. Students still need books, transportation, child care, and rent. These expenses, not tuition, are what force many students to work long hours and eventually quit. Free tuition does nothing about any of them.

And free does not mean finished. Nationally, fewer than half of community college students earn a degree or certificate within six years. Removing tuition will not change that. I have taught writing at a community college for eighteen years, and I have seen what happens when something is given away. One semester, our college waived its registration fee. My classes filled up in August, and by October half the seats were empty. Students value what they pay for, and they do not value what they get for nothing.

Finally, we should consider where this road leads. If community college becomes free, it will not be long before people demand free four-year degrees, then free graduate school, and soon the government will be paying for everyone's education for life. Taxpayers cannot afford that, and neither can our children.

There are better ways to help. Communities could offer emergency grants for car repairs or child care, the kinds of costs that actually drive students out of school. Colleges could hire more advisers to help students choose a path and stay on it. These targeted solutions would help the students who need it most without handing a blank check to everyone else.

stimuli.title: Living on Almost Nothing: How Desert Life Survives
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] A desert is defined less by heat than by dryness. Scientists generally classify a region as a desert if it receives less than about 10 inches of precipitation in a typical year, and some deserts receive far less. By that standard, most of Antarctica, one of the coldest places on Earth, is a desert. In the hot deserts of the American Southwest, the challenge is doubled: rain is scarce, and the sun quickly evaporates the little water that falls. Yet these places are far from empty. Thousands of species of plants and animals survive there by using strategies that fall into three broad groups: storing water, saving water, and avoiding the driest times altogether.

[2] The saguaro cactus is a master of storage. Its thick stem is folded into accordion-like pleats that allow it to swell when rain falls and shrink as the plant uses up its reserves. Its roots spread out in a wide, shallow network only a few inches below the surface, exactly where a brief rain soaks in, and after a single heavy storm a large saguaro may take in hundreds of gallons of water. Some animals store water, too. The desert tortoise can hold water in its bladder and draw on that supply for many months during dry periods.

[3] Other organisms concentrate on saving the water they have. Most plants lose water through tiny pores in their leaves and stems called stomata. Cacti keep their stomata closed during the heat of the day and open them at night, when the cooler air causes far less water to evaporate. A cactus's spines, which are modified leaves, have very little surface area from which water can escape, and they also shade the stem. The creosote bush coats its small leaves in a waxy resin that slows evaporation. Among animals, the kangaroo rat is a champion of saving water. It can live its entire life without drinking. It gets some water from the dry seeds it eats, and much more from the chemical reactions that break down food inside its body, which produce water as a by-product. Its kidneys produce extremely concentrated urine, and its nasal passages cool the air it breathes out so that moisture condenses and is reabsorbed instead of escaping.

[4] A third strategy is simply to avoid the harshest conditions. Many desert animals are nocturnal, spending the hottest hours in burrows that stay much cooler than the surface. Couch's spadefoot toad takes avoidance even further. It spends most of the year buried underground, sometimes for many months at a time, waiting for summer storms. When heavy rain finally arrives, the toads emerge, mate, and lay eggs in temporary pools, often within a single night. The tadpoles can develop into young toads in less than two weeks, fast enough to escape before the puddles dry. Many desert wildflowers follow a similar schedule. Their seeds can wait in the soil for years until enough rain falls; then the plants sprout, bloom, and produce new seeds within a few weeks.

[5] Some plants combine strategies. The mesquite tree sends a taproot straight down, sometimes more than 100 feet, to reach groundwater that surface plants cannot touch. During a severe drought, it may also drop its leaves to reduce water loss until conditions improve.

[6] These adaptations developed over many generations through natural selection, and they are closely matched to the conditions in which they evolved. That is why scientists are watching closely as desert climates change. A young saguaro, for example, needs shade from a “nurse” plant and a few unusually wet years in a row to become established. If droughts grow longer and summers grow hotter, those favorable years may come less often, and even one of the desert's best-adapted species could struggle to replace itself.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: The 911 system grew from a simple idea about one emergency number into a nationwide service that has been updated as technology changed.
A small Alabama telephone company deserves most of the credit for creating the 911 system.
The United States adopted a single emergency number more quickly than other countries did.
Cell phones have made 911 less reliable than it was when most callers used landlines.
items.explain:
The passage traces 911 from the problem of many numbers (paragraph 1), to the decision to adopt one number (paragraphs 2–4), to its slow spread (paragraph 5) and its later improvements for Enhanced 911, cell phones, and texting (paragraphs 6–8). That whole arc is the central idea.

The Alabama company appears in only one paragraph. The passage says London had 999 in 1937, decades before the United States, so the U.S. was not faster. Cell phones created a location problem that is still being worked on, but the passage does not say 911 became less reliable overall.
why: The Alabama Telephone Company appears only in paragraph 4, and it placed the first call; it did not create the system. A detail from one paragraph cannot be the central idea.
Paragraph 2 says London introduced 999 in 1937, about 30 years before the United States chose 911, so the U.S. was slower, not faster.
Paragraph 7 says cell phones created a location problem that is still being worked on, but the passage never says 911 became less reliable overall. This is one detail, not the main idea.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 1?
options: to argue that telephone operators gave poor service
to describe the problem that a single emergency number was meant to solve
to compare the costs of fire, police, and ambulance services
to explain why AT&T chose the digits 9-1-1
items.explain:
Paragraph 1 shows how confusing it was to get help: separate numbers for fire, police, and ambulance, operators busy with other requests, and “dozens of different emergency numbers” in large areas. This is the problem that the rest of the passage shows 911 solving.

The paragraph mentions operators but does not attack them; it explains that they handled “every kind of request.” Costs are never compared, and the choice of 9-1-1 is explained in paragraph 3.
why: Paragraph 1 mentions operators only to show they handled “every kind of request,” so emergency callers could wait. It explains a problem with the system; it does not attack the operators.
No costs are compared in paragraph 1. It lists the different numbers a caller had to know, which is the problem a single number solved.
The choice of 9-1-1 is explained in paragraph 3, not paragraph 1. Paragraph 1 sets up the problem before any number was chosen.

items.prompt: Paragraph 3 is shown below. Click the sentence that best explains why 9-1-1 could be introduced without forcing any customers to change the phone numbers they already had.
spans: The telephone industry then had to choose the digits.
In January 1968, AT&T, which operated most of the nation's phone lines, announced that the number would be 9-1-1.
It was short and easy to remember.
It had also never been used as an area code or as the first three digits of a local phone number, so it would not conflict with numbers already in service.
On the rotary-dial phones of the time, it could be dialed fairly quickly while still being unlikely to be dialed by accident.
items.explain:
Because 9-1-1 “had also never been used as an area code or as the first three digits of a local phone number,” it “would not conflict with numbers already in service.” No existing number had to change.

The sentences about being easy to remember and quick to dial on rotary phones describe other advantages, but they do not address existing phone numbers.
items.why: Many students click “It was short and easy to remember,” but that is about convenience, not existing numbers. Only the sentence saying 9-1-1 had never been used as an area code or the first three digits of a local number explains why no one had to change numbers.

items.prompt: Paragraph 4 says the Alabama Telephone Company “raced to beat the giant to the milestone.” What does this detail suggest about the company?
options: It had been ordered by Congress to test the 911 system.
It operated more phone lines in Alabama than AT&T did.
It wanted the recognition of completing the first 911 call before the much larger AT&T could.
It disagreed with AT&T's choice of the digits 9-1-1.
items.explain:
The company “raced to beat the giant to the milestone” and its crews “worked quickly.” Racing to be first suggests it wanted the credit for the historic first call.

Nothing in the paragraph says Congress ordered the test, compares the number of lines each company ran, or suggests the company objected to the digits; in fact, it used them.
why: Paragraph 4 never mentions Congress ordering a test; a congressman only received the ceremonial call. The word “raced” points to the company's own desire to be first.
Paragraph 3 says AT&T operated most of the nation's lines, and paragraph 4 calls it “the giant,” so the small company did not have more lines.
The company used the digits 9-1-1 for its call, so it did not object to them. “Raced to beat the giant” shows it wanted the credit of going first.

items.prompt: Arrange these milestones in the history of 911 from earliest to latest. Drag each milestone into its correct place on the timeline.
choices: AT&T announces that the emergency number will be 9-1-1.
Congress designates 911 as the universal emergency number for all telephone service.
A presidential commission urges the country to adopt one number for all emergencies.
The first 911 call is placed in Haleyville, Alabama.
A national association of fire chiefs recommends one number for reporting fires.
items.explain:
The dates in the passage give the order: (1) fire chiefs' recommendation, 1957; (2) presidential commission, 1967; (3) AT&T's announcement, January 1968; (4) first call in Haleyville, February 16, 1968; (5) Congress's law, 1999.

Be careful with the two 1968 events: the announcement came in January, and the first call came in February.
items.why: The most common mistake is swapping the two 1968 events. Paragraph 3 says AT&T announced 9-1-1 in January 1968, and paragraph 4 dates the Haleyville call to February 16, 1968, so the announcement comes first.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author writes, “Progress was uneven.” As used here, uneven most nearly means—
options: unfair to some callers
poorly built
rough on the surface
happening at different speeds in different places
items.explain:
The colon after “Progress was uneven” introduces the explanation: some large cities adopted 911 “within a few years,” while many rural areas “waited until the 1990s or later.” Uneven means the change happened at different speeds in different places.

“Rough on the surface” is the literal meaning of the word, which does not fit progress. The paragraph says nothing about fairness or poor construction.
why: Paragraph 5 does not discuss fairness. The sentences after “Progress was uneven” contrast cities that adopted 911 “within a few years” with rural areas that waited until the 1990s, which is about speed.
Nothing in paragraph 5 says the systems were badly built. The paragraph is about when different places got 911.
“Rough on the surface” is the literal meaning of uneven, which does not fit “progress.” Context shows it means progress came at different speeds in different places.

items.prompt: According to paragraphs 6 and 7, which problems with the 911 system were engineers and lawmakers trying to solve? Select two answers.
options: Callers often dialed 911 by accident on rotary phones.
Early 911 gave dispatchers no information about where a caller was.
Telephone companies refused to add 911 fees to customers' bills.
Mobile phones are not linked to a fixed street address.
Operators were sending fire calls to the police.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 says early 911 “told a dispatcher nothing about the caller,” which Enhanced 911 fixed by displaying the number and address. Paragraph 7 explains that a mobile phone “has no fixed address,” so laws and regulations required carriers to send location data.

Paragraph 3 says 9-1-1 was “unlikely to be dialed by accident.” The passage never says companies refused fees or that operators misrouted calls.
why: Paragraph 3 says 9-1-1 was “unlikely to be dialed by accident,” and this point is not in paragraphs 6 or 7. It was not a problem engineers were fixing.
Paragraph 5 says many communities funded 911 with a fee on phone bills; nowhere does the passage say companies refused. It is also not in paragraphs 6 or 7.
Paragraph 1 says operators handled every kind of request, but the passage never says they sent fire calls to the police, and that detail is not in paragraphs 6 or 7.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how the passage is organized?
options: It presents arguments for and against a national emergency number.
It follows the development of 911 in time order, from its origins to the present.
It compares the U.S. emergency system with systems in several other countries.
It lists changes to 911 from the most important to the least important.
items.explain:
The passage moves forward in time: the early twentieth century, 1937, 1957, 1967, 1968, the 1970s and 1980s, 1999, 2022, and “today.” That is chronological order.

The author never argues against 911. London's 999 is the only other system mentioned, so the passage is not a comparison of several countries. The changes are presented by date, not ranked by importance.
why: The author never argues against a national number; the passage reports events and their dates rather than weighing pros and cons.
London's 999 (paragraph 2) is the only other system mentioned, so the passage does not compare several countries.
The changes appear in the order they happened (1970s–1980s, 1999, 2022), not ranked from most to least important.

items.prompt: Which conclusion about the 988 number is best supported by paragraph 8?
options: It replaced 911 for most callers who use cell phones.
It was created because 911 call centers could not accept text messages.
It reflects the idea that some emergencies are better handled by trained counselors than by the usual 911 response.
It was the first three-digit emergency number used in the United States.
items.explain:
Paragraph 8 says 988 is “a separate three-digit number” for people “experiencing a mental health crisis,” so that “those callers can reach trained counselors.” Creating a separate line for one kind of emergency shows the belief that such calls may be better answered by specialists.

It is “separate,” so it did not replace 911. Texting to 911 is described as already available in many areas. And 911 itself is a three-digit number that began in 1968, long before 988.
why: Paragraph 8 calls 988 “a separate three-digit number” for mental health crises; it did not replace 911, which still handles about 240 million calls a year.
Paragraph 8 says many areas already let people text 911. The reason given for 988 is so crisis callers “can reach trained counselors,” not a texting problem.
911 is itself a three-digit number and began in 1968 (paragraphs 3–4), so 988, launched in 2022, was not the first.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“We have received 23 reports of switches melting{{0}} two customers reported minor burns to their hands.”

options: , two customers reported
two customers reported
, and two customers reported
, which two customers reported
why: A comma alone between two complete sentences is a comma splice. Add a coordinating conjunction: “melting, and two customers reported.”
With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on). Join them with a comma and “and.”
“Which” has nothing it can logically refer to; customers did not report the melting switches as burns. The second part is its own clause, so join it with “, and.”

items.explain:
Both parts of the sentence are independent clauses (“We have received 23 reports …” and “two customers reported minor burns …”). Two independent clauses can be joined with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction: melting, and two customers reported.

A comma alone creates a comma splice, and no punctuation creates a run-on. “Which two customers reported” makes no sense, because “which” has nothing it can logically refer to.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The affected heaters, which are gray with a black front grille, {{0}} the model number PH-15 printed on a white label under the base.”

options: has
have
having
is having
why: “Has” is singular, but the subject is “heaters,” which is plural. Skip the “which” clause and match the verb to “heaters”: have.
“Having” is not a complete verb, so the sentence would have no main verb. The plural subject “heaters” needs “have.”
“Is having” is singular and is the wrong tense for a simple fact. The plural subject “heaters” needs “have.”

items.explain:
The subject is heaters, which is plural, so the verb must be plural: have. The clause “which are gray with a black front grille” sits between the subject and verb but does not change the subject.

“Has” and “is having” are singular, and “having” cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Check that label before you do anything else; {{0}} model number and date code appear in the lower right corner.”

options: it's
its
its'
their
why: “It's” means “it is,” and “it is model number” makes no sense. The model number belongs to the label, so use the possessive “its.”
“Its'” is not a word in standard English. The possessive form of “it” has no apostrophe: its.
“Their” is plural, but it refers to one label. Use the singular possessive “its.”

items.explain:
The sentence needs a possessive pronoun referring to the label (the model number and date code belong to the label): its.

“It's” is a contraction of “it is,” which does not fit. “Its'” is never correct. “Their” is plural, but “label” is singular.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“This problem does not {{0}} heaters with model numbers that begin with PH-20.”

options: effect
affect
effects
affects
why: “Effect” is usually a noun meaning a result. Here the sentence needs a verb meaning “to influence”: affect.
After the helping verb “does,” use the base verb, and “effects” is a noun anyway. The correct word is “affect.”
“Affects” is the right word but the wrong form. After “does not,” use the base form: affect.

items.explain:
The sentence needs a verb meaning “to influence or change”: affect. After the helping verb “does,” the base form is used, so “affects” is incorrect.

“Effect” and “effects” are usually nouns meaning “a result.”

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes the second sentence.

“Customers should stop using the recalled heaters immediately. {{0}}, they should not throw the heaters away, because we need the date code to process each refund.”

options: However
Therefore
For example
Similarly
why: “Therefore” signals a result, but keeping the heater does not follow from stopping its use. The second sentence warns against an expected next step, which is a contrast: However.
“For example” introduces an illustration, but not throwing the heater away is not an example of stopping its use. The idea contrasts with what readers might expect: However.
“Similarly” signals a likeness, but the second instruction cuts against the expected action of throwing the heater out. Use a contrast word: However.

items.explain:
The first sentence says to stop using the heaters; the second warns readers not to take the next step they might expect, throwing them away. That contrast calls for However.

“Therefore” would mean that keeping the heater is a result of stopping its use. “For example” and “Similarly” signal an illustration or a likeness, not a contrast.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“To receive a full refund, visit our website, enter the date code, and {{0}}.”

options: a prepaid shipping label will be printed
printing the prepaid shipping label
print the prepaid shipping label
you should be printing the label
why: This switches to the passive voice, breaking the series of commands “visit … enter ….” The third item must also begin with a base verb: print.
The -ing form “printing” does not match “visit” and “enter.” Items in a series need parallel form: print the prepaid shipping label.
Adding “you should be printing” brings in a new subject and verb form, which breaks the parallel series of commands. Use “print the prepaid shipping label.”

items.explain:
The first two items in the series are commands that begin with a base verb: “visit our website,” “enter the date code.” The third item must match: print the prepaid shipping label.

The other choices switch to the passive voice, an -ing form, or a new subject, which breaks the parallel structure.

items.prompt:
Choose the sentence that is written correctly and should be placed in blank (7) of the notice.

{{0}}

options: Packed in its original box if possible, customers should return the heater using the prepaid label.
Customers should return the heater, packed in its original box if possible, using the prepaid label.
Customers packed in the original box should return the heater using the prepaid label.
Using the prepaid label, the heater should be returned by customers packed in its original box.
why: The opening phrase “Packed in its original box” sits next to “customers,” so it says the customers are packed in a box (a dangling modifier).
This says the customers are packed in the original box. The phrase must describe the heater, so place it right after “the heater.”
This says the heater is “using the prepaid label” and puts “packed in its original box” next to “customers.” Both modifiers are misplaced.

items.explain:
A modifier must sit next to the word it describes. In the correct sentence, “packed in its original box if possible” comes right after the heater, and “using the prepaid label” clearly describes how customers return it.

In the first choice, the opening phrase describes “customers,” so it says the customers are packed in a box. The third choice says the same thing directly. The fourth choice says the heater is using the label and places “packed in its original box” next to “customers.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Customers who bought a heater at {{0}} may instead return it to any store location for an immediate refund.”

options: Pine Valley hardware
Pine Valley Hardware
pine valley Hardware
Pine valley Hardware
why: “Hardware” is part of the store's name, so it must be capitalized too: Pine Valley Hardware.
“Pine” and “Valley” are part of a proper noun and must be capitalized.
“Valley” is part of the business name and must be capitalized: Pine Valley Hardware.

items.explain:
The name of a specific business is a proper noun, so every important word is capitalized: Pine Valley Hardware.

The other choices leave one or more words of the store's name in lowercase.

items.prompt: Why does Nell hesitate before reporting the smoke?
options: She believes Walt would want to report it himself.
She cannot find the correct bearing on the fire finder.
She thinks the radio dispatcher is unfriendly to new lookouts.
She is afraid of being embarrassed by another false report.
items.explain:
Paragraphs 4 and 5 show her worry: she has “already called in one false smoke,” she remembers Walt's warning that dispatch will “tell the whole district,” and she fears she “would be the girl who cried smoke, twice.”

Walt has left the tower. She finds the bearing without trouble in paragraph 8. The dispatcher's voice is described as “patient,” not unfriendly.
why: Paragraph 2 says Walt was sent down the mountain because of his eyesight; he is gone and cannot report anything. Nell reads his logbook for guidance, not because he wants to report it himself.
Paragraph 8 shows she lines up the crosshair and reads the bearing without trouble. Her delay comes before she uses the fire finder.
Paragraph 4 describes the dispatcher's voice as “patient,” and in paragraph 10 dispatch sends an engine right away. Her worry is about her own reputation.

items.prompt: In paragraph 1, the forest is compared to “a rumpled green blanket,” and Nell believes she knows “every fold.” What does this comparison mainly suggest?
options: The landscape is vast and uneven, and Nell has studied it closely.
The forest has been damaged and left untidy by logging.
Nell feels sleepy and bored during her long shifts.
The mountains are covered with fresh snow.
items.explain:
A rumpled blanket has many ridges and hollows, like a mountain landscape seen from above. Saying Nell knows “every fold” after “six weeks” of staring shows she has studied every ridge and valley closely.

The comparison is about the shape of the land, not damage. Nothing suggests she is sleepy; she is alert throughout. The blanket is “green,” so it does not describe snow.
why: Nothing in paragraph 1 mentions logging damage. “Rumpled” describes the ridges and valleys, and “every fold” shows how closely Nell has studied them.
A blanket can suggest sleep, but Nell has been “staring at it for six weeks” and spots a thin thread of smoke, so she is alert, not bored.
The blanket is “green,” and the story takes place in a hot July, so the comparison is not about snow.

items.prompt: Part of the story is shown below. Click the sentence that most directly leads Nell to change her mind and report the smoke.
spans: She opened Walt's logbook instead, flipping back through years of entries, looking for a sign of what he would do.
July 1994: Smoke, Dutchman, NE slope. Reported 15:20. Lightning strike. Crew on scene 17:45.
August 2003: Possible smoke, Dutchman. Watched 20 min. Thought dust. Not reported.
Below that, in different ink, as if added later: Not dust. Should have called it. Better a dozen false alarms than one late one.
She had always imagined Walt as someone who was never wrong, someone who simply knew.
items.explain:
Walt's later note admits that the 2003 smoke was real and that he “should have called it,” and it states the lesson: “Better a dozen false alarms than one late one.” Right after reading this line twice, Nell takes her bearing and picks up the radio.

The 2003 entry shows Walt's mistake, but only the added note tells Nell what he learned from it. The other sentences describe her searching and her old view of Walt.
items.why: Many students click the August 2003 entry, but it only records that Walt thought it was dust and did not report it. The sentence added later, “Should have called it. Better a dozen false alarms than one late one,” gives the lesson that pushes Nell to pick up the radio.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: People should trust equipment more than their own judgment.
Older workers should step aside so younger workers can learn.
Even experienced people feel uncertain, and acting responsibly matters more than avoiding embarrassment.
Nature is too powerful for people to control.
items.explain:
Nell learns that Walt, whom she thought “never wrong,” was also once “unsure” and regretted not calling. She chooses to report the smoke despite her fear of looking foolish, and her report catches a real fire. The story's message is that doing the responsible thing outweighs the risk of embarrassment.

The fire finder helps, but the key decision is hers. Walt leaves because of his eyesight, not because the story argues that older workers should step aside. The fire is quickly contained, so the story does not show nature as uncontrollable.
why: Nell uses the fire finder to measure, but the key turn is her decision after reading Walt's note. The story is about her judgment and courage, not about trusting equipment over judgment.
Walt leaves because “his eyes had grown too cloudy,” not to make room for younger workers. Nell still learns from him through the logbook.
The fire is “Quarter acre, contained” within about an hour, so the story shows people controlling it. The focus is Nell's choice to act despite fear.

items.prompt: How does Nell's view of Walt change in paragraph 7?
options: She begins to resent him for leaving her alone at the tower.
She realizes that he, too, sometimes doubted himself.
She decides that he kept careless records in the logbook.
She concludes that his training is out of date.
items.explain:
Nell “had always imagined Walt as someone who was never wrong,” but the logbook shows he once stood “in this same spot … unsure.” She now sees him as a person who also felt doubt.

She shows no resentment. His records are careful enough that she learns from them, and nothing suggests his training was out of date.
why: Paragraph 7 shows surprise, not resentment. Walt left because of his eyesight, and Nell turns to his logbook for help.
Paragraph 6 shows Walt's entries are detailed, with times and outcomes, and Nell learns from them. Nothing calls his records careless.
Nothing suggests his training was out of date. Paragraph 7 is about Nell learning that even Walt was once “unsure.”

items.prompt: Which details from the story best show that Nell handles the smoke report like a skilled lookout? Select two answers.
options: She once reported steam from a hot spring as smoke.
She checks the bearing on the fire finder more than once before calling.
Her handwriting is rounder than Walt's.
Her radio report gives the bearing, the distance, and a description of the smoke.
She opens the logbook before calling dispatch.
Walt received a cake and a plaque when he left.
items.explain:
In paragraph 8 she “read the bearing, checked it, and read it again,” and in paragraph 9 her report is precise: “bearing two-one-four, approximately six miles, just beyond the Dutchman. Small, bluish gray, steady.” Both show careful, skilled work.

The hot-spring report was a mistake. Her handwriting, Walt's going-away gifts, and her delay while reading the logbook do not show skill in making the report.
why: The hot-spring steam (paragraph 4) was a false report, a mistake, so it does not show skill.
Her rounder handwriting (paragraph 12) describes how she writes, not how well she handled the report.
Opening the logbook (paragraph 6) delayed her call while she searched for reassurance; it shows her doubt, not her skill at reporting.
Walt's cake and plaque (paragraph 2) are about his retirement and have nothing to do with Nell's report.

items.prompt: Why does the author include the dispatcher's earlier words, “Copy that, Juniper, we'll make a note,” in paragraph 4?
options: to show that dispatchers do not take lookouts' reports seriously
to explain the steps a lookout follows when reporting smoke
to reveal that Nell has been warned she could lose her job
to show why Nell fears that a second mistaken report would hurt her reputation
items.explain:
The line recalls her earlier false report. Combined with Walt's warning that dispatch will “tell the whole district,” the remembered words explain her fear of being known as “the girl who cried smoke, twice.”

The dispatcher immediately sends an engine when Nell calls, so dispatch does take reports seriously. The line does not explain reporting steps, and no one threatens her job.
why: In paragraph 10, dispatch replies “Sending an engine to check it out,” so dispatch does take reports seriously. The remembered line explains Nell's embarrassment, not dispatch's attitude.
The line is a reply to her earlier false report, not a list of steps. The steps of reporting appear in paragraphs 8 and 9.
No one threatens her job. The line, together with Walt's warning that dispatch will “tell the whole district,” shows she fears looking foolish.

items.prompt: In the final paragraph, why does Nell most likely turn back to Walt's August 2003 note before closing the logbook?
options: She recognizes that his lesson guided her decision, and she feels connected to him through it.
She wants to correct a mistake in the date of his entry.
She is checking whether the 2003 fire was in the same place as today's fire.
She plans to show the note to dispatch as proof that she was right.
items.explain:
Walt's note convinced her to make the call, and the call proved correct. After writing her own entry, she reads “his note one more time,” a quiet act that shows gratitude and a sense that she is continuing his work, much as her entry now sits in the same book as his.

Nothing suggests an error in his date or a need to compare locations, and the dispatcher has already said “Good catch,” so she has no need for proof.
why: Nothing in the story suggests Walt's date is wrong; she reads the note “one more time,” a quiet act of reflection, not correction.
Both smokes were near the Dutchman, but she has already written today's outcome. Rereading the note shows what it meant to her, not a location check.
Dispatch already said “Good catch, Juniper,” so she needs no proof. She rereads the note because his lesson guided her choice.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a supporter and a critic of making community college tuition-free.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Renata Olsen's reference letter?

“The company's owner and {{0}} both came to depend on her.”

options: me
I
myself
mine
why: “Me” is an object pronoun, but here it is part of the subject of “came.” Test it alone: “I came to depend on her,” not “me came.”
“Myself” is used only when “I” already appears in the sentence. As part of the subject, use “I.”
“Mine” shows possession and cannot be a subject here. The subject form is “I.”

items.explain:
The pronoun is part of the compound subject of the verb “came,” so it must be in the subject case: I. Test it by removing the other person: “I came to depend on her,” not “Me came.”

“Myself” is used only when the subject has already been named (“I did it myself”), and “mine” shows possession.

items.prompt:
Choose the sentence that is written correctly and should be placed in blank (2) of the letter.

{{0}}

options: Especially during the spring, when the phones never stopped ringing and the line stretched out the door.
Jordan kept that counter running smoothly, even in the spring, when the line stretched out the door.
Jordan keeping that counter running smoothly, even in the spring, when the line stretched out the door.
Jordan kept that counter running smoothly, the line stretched out the door in the spring.
why: This has no subject or main verb, so it is a sentence fragment. The sentence needs “Jordan kept …”
“Keeping” without a helping verb is not a complete verb, so this is a fragment. Use “Jordan kept.”
This joins two complete sentences with only a comma, a comma splice. The correct choice attaches the spring detail as a phrase.

items.explain:
The correct choice has a subject (“Jordan”) and a complete verb (“kept”), and the added phrases are properly attached with commas.

The first choice has no subject or main verb, so it is a fragment. The third choice uses “keeping” without a helping verb, which is also a fragment. The fourth choice joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice.

items.prompt:
Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Renata Olsen's reference letter?

“She also learned the names and care needs of our plants faster {{0}} anyone I have trained in my twelve years as store supervisor.”

options: then
than
that
then even
why: “Then” refers to time or order. A comparison such as “faster … anyone” needs “than.”
“That” does not complete a comparison. After “faster,” use “than.”
“Then even” still uses the time word “then.” A comparison needs “than.”

items.explain:
The sentence makes a comparison (“faster … anyone”), so it needs than.

“Then” refers to time or sequence (“first this, then that”), and “that” does not complete a comparison.

items.prompt:
Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Renata Olsen's reference letter?

“Within a few months, she was the person {{0}} new employees asked for help.”

options: who
whom
which
whose
why: “Who” is a subject form, but the subject of the clause is “new employees.” The pronoun is the object of “asked” (they asked her), so use “whom.”
“Which” is used for things, not people. For a person who receives the action, use “whom.”
“Whose” shows possession, but nothing belongs to the person here. Employees asked her, so use the object form “whom.”

items.explain:
In the clause “___ new employees asked for help,” the subject is “new employees,” and the pronoun is the object of “asked” (new employees asked her). Object pronouns take the form whom. A quick test: if you can answer with “him” or “her,” use “whom.”

“Who” is the subject form. “Which” is not used for people, and “whose” shows possession.

items.prompt:
Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Renata Olsen's reference letter?

“She remembered many of our regular {{0}} names and the plants they had bought, and customers noticed.”

options: customer's
customers'
customers
customers's
why: “Customer's” is singular possessive, but the letter says “many” customers. For a plural noun ending in s, add only an apostrophe: customers'.
“Customers” with no apostrophe is a plain plural. The names belong to the customers, so it needs the possessive apostrophe: customers'.
“Customers's” is not standard. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe: customers'.

items.explain:
The names belong to many customers, so the word must be a plural possessive. For a plural noun ending in s, add only an apostrophe: customers'.

“Customer's” is singular possessive, but “many” customers are meant. “Customers” has no apostrophe to show possession, and “customers's” is not a standard form.

items.prompt:
Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Renata Olsen's reference letter?

“Last year, she {{0}} a color-coded care-tag system that cut plant returns by nearly a third.”

options: creates
has been creating
created
will create
why: “Creates” is present tense, but “Last year” and “cut” place the action in the past. Use “created.”
“Has been creating” describes an action still going on, but the system was finished last year. Use simple past: created.
“Will create” is future tense, which clashes with “Last year.” Use “created.”

items.explain:
“Last year” places the action in a completed past time, and the rest of the sentence uses the past tense (“cut”). The verb should be simple past: created.

“Creates” is present, “will create” is future, and “has been creating” describes an action still going on.

items.prompt:
Which choice correctly completes the second of these two sentences from Renata Olsen's reference letter?

“Jordan is leaving our company only because she is moving closer to her family. {{0}}, I would hire her again without hesitation.”

options: As a result
In fact
Instead
For instance
why: “As a result” would mean she would rehire Jordan because Jordan is moving, which makes no sense. The second sentence adds emphasis: In fact.
“Instead” signals a replacement or alternative, but the second sentence builds on the first. Use “In fact.”
“For instance” introduces an example, but rehiring is not an example of moving. The sentence strengthens the praise: In fact.

items.explain:
The second sentence strengthens the first: Jordan is not leaving because of any problem, and the writer goes further to say she would rehire her. In fact signals that kind of emphasis.

“As a result” would mean the writer would rehire her because she is moving. “Instead” signals a replacement, and “For instance” introduces an example.

items.prompt:
Which choice correctly completes this sentence from Renata Olsen's reference letter?

“If you would like another perspective, I am happy to put you in touch with {{0}}, our owner, who worked beside her almost daily.”

options: ms. Grace Whitfield
Ms. grace Whitfield
Ms. Grace Whitfield
Ms. Grace whitfield
why: The title “Ms.” must be capitalized when it comes before a name.
“Grace” is a first name, a proper noun, and must be capitalized.
“Whitfield” is a last name, a proper noun, and must be capitalized.

items.explain:
A title used before a name is capitalized, and both parts of a person's name are proper nouns: Ms. Grace Whitfield.

Each of the other choices leaves the title, the first name, or the last name in lowercase.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Deserts are defined mainly by their extremely high temperatures.
The saguaro cactus is the best-adapted living thing in the desert.
Desert plants and animals survive through adaptations that help them store water, save water, or avoid the driest times.
Changes in climate will soon wipe out most desert species.
items.explain:
Paragraph 1 names the three strategies, “storing water, saving water, and avoiding the driest times,” and paragraphs 2–5 give examples of each. That is the central idea.

Paragraph 1 says a desert is defined “less by heat than by dryness.” The saguaro is one example among many. Paragraph 6 says some species “could struggle,” which is far weaker than “wipe out most desert species.”
why: Paragraph 1 says a desert is defined “less by heat than by dryness” and even calls cold Antarctica a desert, so heat is not the main idea.
The saguaro is one example of the storing strategy in paragraph 2. The passage never ranks it as the best-adapted living thing.
Paragraph 6 says species “could struggle,” a cautious claim. “Wipe out most desert species” overstates it.

items.prompt: The passage describes three survival strategies. Drag each example into the strategy it illustrates.
choices: A saguaro's pleated stem swells after rain.
A cactus opens its stomata only at night.
A spadefoot toad stays buried underground for months.
A creosote bush's leaves are coated in waxy resin.
A desert tortoise keeps water in its bladder.
Wildflower seeds wait in the soil for years.
items.explain:
Storing water (paragraph 2): the saguaro's swelling stem and the tortoise's bladder hold water for later use.

Saving water (paragraph 3): opening stomata at night and coating leaves in resin both reduce how much water escapes.

Avoiding dry times (paragraph 4): the spadefoot toad waits underground and wildflower seeds wait in the soil until rain comes.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the cactus opening its stomata at night under Avoiding dry times because it involves night. The cactus is still active; it is cutting water loss, which is Saving water (paragraph 3). The toad and wildflower seeds avoid dry times by waiting for rain.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 3, why is opening its stomata at night an advantage for a cactus?
options: Sunlight damages open stomata during the day.
Less water evaporates from the plant in the cooler night air.
Animals that eat cacti are less active at night.
Most desert rain falls at night.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 says cacti open their stomata at night, “when the cooler air causes far less water to evaporate.” Opening the pores only then saves water.

The passage does not mention sunlight damaging stomata, animals eating cacti, or rain falling mostly at night.
why: Paragraph 3 never says sunlight damages stomata. The reason given is that cooler night air “causes far less water to evaporate.”
The passage does not mention animals eating cacti. Paragraph 3 ties night opening to less evaporation.
The passage does not say when rain falls. The advantage is that less water evaporates in the cooler night air.

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, the author says the chemical reactions that break down food “produce water as a by-product.” As used here, by-product means—
options: a waste material that harms the body
a food item stored for later use
a step that must happen before a process can begin
something produced in addition to the main result of a process
items.explain:
The main purpose of breaking down food is to release energy, but the reactions also “produce water.” A by-product is something made along the way in addition to the main result.

The water is useful to the kangaroo rat, not harmful. It is not stored food, and it comes from the process rather than before it.
why: The water is useful to the kangaroo rat, not harmful; paragraph 3 says it supplies “much more” of its water than its food.
Nothing is stored; the water is made as food is broken down. A by-product comes out of a process along with its main result.
The water is made during the breakdown of food, not before it begins, so it is not a first step.

items.prompt: Why does the author mention Antarctica in paragraph 1?
options: to emphasize that a desert is defined by low precipitation rather than by heat
to show that deserts are found on every continent
to contrast the animals of cold deserts with those of hot deserts
to suggest that hot deserts receive more rain than cold deserts
items.explain:
Right after saying a desert is defined “less by heat than by dryness,” the author points out that Antarctica, “one of the coldest places on Earth,” is a desert. The surprising example makes the point that dryness, not heat, is what counts.

The passage does not list continents, never discusses Antarctic animals, and never compares rainfall in hot and cold deserts.
why: The passage mentions only Antarctica and the American Southwest; it never says deserts are on every continent.
Paragraph 1 never discusses Antarctic animals. Antarctica appears right after the line that deserts are defined by dryness, not heat.
The passage never compares rainfall in hot and cold deserts. Antarctica is used to show that a cold place can still be a desert.

items.prompt: Which statements about the kangaroo rat are supported by the passage? Select two answers.
options: It drinks from temporary pools after summer storms.
It gets water from its food and from chemical reactions in its own body.
It stores extra water in its bladder for many months.
It is active mainly during the hottest part of the day.
Its body reduces the amount of water lost when it breathes out.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 says the kangaroo rat “gets some water from the dry seeds it eats, and much more from the chemical reactions that break down food,” and that its nasal passages cause moisture in exhaled air to be “reabsorbed instead of escaping.”

It “can live its entire life without drinking,” so it does not need pools. Storing water in the bladder describes the desert tortoise. The passage never says it is active in the hottest hours.
why: Paragraph 3 says the kangaroo rat “can live its entire life without drinking.” Laying eggs in temporary pools describes the spadefoot toad.
Storing water in its bladder describes the desert tortoise (paragraph 2), not the kangaroo rat.
The passage never says the kangaroo rat is active in the hottest hours; paragraph 4 says many desert animals avoid the heat, and the table lists it as active at night.

items.prompt: How does the mesquite tree's way of getting water differ from the saguaro's?
options: The mesquite stores water in pleated stems, while the saguaro drops its leaves.
The mesquite gets water only from rain, while the saguaro uses groundwater.
The mesquite reaches deep groundwater, while the saguaro collects rain near the surface.
The mesquite takes in water only at night, while the saguaro takes it in during the day.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 says the mesquite's taproot goes down “sometimes more than 100 feet, to reach groundwater.” Paragraph 2 says the saguaro's roots spread “only a few inches below the surface, exactly where a brief rain soaks in.”

The first two choices reverse or mix up the details. The passage says nothing about when either plant absorbs water from the soil.
why: This mixes up the details. The pleated stem belongs to the saguaro (paragraph 2), and dropping leaves describes the mesquite (paragraph 5).
This reverses the plants. Paragraph 5 says the mesquite reaches groundwater; paragraph 2 says the saguaro's shallow roots catch rain.
The passage says nothing about when either plant takes in water through its roots. Night activity is mentioned for cactus stomata, which release water, not absorb it.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by paragraph 6?
options: Saguaros will disappear from the Southwest within a few years.
Nurse plants harm young saguaros by competing with them for water.
Desert species can quickly adapt to any change in climate.
Even species that are well adapted to the desert could struggle if dry periods become longer and hotter.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 explains that adaptations are “closely matched” to past conditions and that young saguaros need “a few unusually wet years in a row.” If droughts lengthen, “even one of the desert's best-adapted species could struggle.”

The author says “could struggle,” not that saguaros will vanish in a few years. Nurse plants help seedlings by giving shade. Adaptations developed “over many generations,” which suggests they cannot change quickly.
why: Paragraph 6 says saguaros “could struggle to replace itself,” a possibility, not a prediction that they will vanish in a few years.
Paragraph 6 says a young saguaro needs shade from a “nurse” plant, so nurse plants help, not harm, seedlings.
Paragraph 6 says adaptations developed “over many generations,” which suggests species cannot change quickly.

items.prompt: According to the table, which animal gets the largest share of its daily water from drinking free water?
options: Coyote
Gambel's quail
Desert tortoise
Kangaroo rat
items.explain:
The “Drinking free water” column shows 0% (kangaroo rat), 5% (jackrabbit), 20% (tortoise), 40% (coyote), and 45% (quail). The largest value, 45%, belongs to Gambel's quail.

The coyote is close at 40%, but 40% is less than 45%.
why: The coyote gets 40% from drinking, which is close but less than the quail's 45%.
The desert tortoise gets only 20% from drinking. Its largest source is moisture in food (75%).
